title: What He Does Not Say
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 12 of 40
content:
Once I learned to hear Snape's silences, he became almost unbearably talkative.

Not in words.

Never in words if a glare would do.

But there were different kinds of quiet.

The quiet when he was concentrating had weight but no edge.

The quiet when pain climbed his throat made his shoulders lift toward his ears.

The quiet when someone mentioned Dumbledore was complicated enough to deserve its own vocabulary.

And the quiet when children passed the dungeon door was the strangest of all.

Hogwarts was not yet open for term, but families had begun arriving to collect belongings left behind during the battle. Former students came with parents, siblings, guardians, and the peculiar bravery of people returning to a place where they had once been afraid.

Most avoided the dungeons.

Some did not.

A boy of perhaps seventeen appeared in the doorway one afternoon while Snape and I were sorting preserved fluxweed.

The boy stopped so abruptly his mother nearly walked into him.

Snape looked up.

The boy went pale.

“Professor.”

Snape's face became unreadable.

“Mr. Hopkins.”

I knew the name from the evidence notes. Hufflepuff. Detention under the Carrows. Broken wrist, healed badly because he had refused to report who had cursed him.

His mother looked between them.

“We only came for his cauldron,” she said.

“Storage room four,” Snape replied.

His voice was formal and cold.

The boy did not move.

Neither did Snape.

Then Hopkins said, “You changed the detention rota.”

Snape's hand stopped over the jar.

His mother frowned. “What?”

The boy kept looking at him.

“In March. They were making us practice curses on first-years. You changed the list and put me in inventory with Filch.”

Snape's expression did not move.

“You were deficient in practical organization.”

Hopkins swallowed.

“You did it three times.”

“Then your deficiency was persistent.”

The boy gave a shaky laugh.

His mother covered her mouth.

Snape looked down at the fluxweed.

“Storage room four,” he repeated.

Hopkins nodded.

“Thank you,” he said.

Snape's fingers tightened around the jar.

“Your cauldron,” he said, “has been awaiting collection for months. I suggest you finally demonstrate responsibility.”

The boy smiled.

Actually smiled.

“Yes, sir.”

They left.

I waited until their footsteps faded.

Snape resumed sorting.

I resumed with him.

Five minutes passed.

Then ten.

I said, “You could have said you're welcome.”

“No.”

“Too dangerous?”

“Yes.”

I glanced at him.

He was not joking.

“Why?”

“Because gratitude is rarely simple after war.”

“That sounded suspiciously wise.”

“It was practical.”

“You don't want him to owe you.”

Snape's eyes flicked toward mine.

There it was.

One of the silences.

I understood.

“You don't,” I said.

“He owes me nothing.”

“You helped him.”

“I reduced his exposure to people I permitted to remain in this school.”

The words were brutal.

Toward himself.

“You didn't permit the Carrows,” I said.

“I was Headmaster.”

“Under Voldemort.”

“I occupied the office.”

“You were also trying to keep students alive.”

“And failed in ways you have not catalogued.”

I set down the jar.

“This is what you do.”

His expression chilled.

“What, precisely?”

“You turn responsibility into total responsibility. If you couldn't prevent everything, then you act as if anything that happened belongs to you.”

His voice lowered. “Do not absolve me.”

“I am not.”

The force of my answer surprised both of us.

“I am not absolving you,” I repeated. “You were cruel to students before the war. You protected Slytherins when they were wrong. You humiliated people who couldn't fight back. You joined Voldemort. You gave him information that led to a family being targeted. Those things are yours.”

His face had gone white.

I kept going because stopping would make the honesty worse.

“So are the altered detention rosters. The fake compliance draughts. The warnings. The counter-curses. The things you did when nobody could thank you. You do not get to keep only the worst evidence because it fits the sentence you've already passed on yourself.”

For a moment I thought he might hex me.

Instead he laughed.

It was a terrible sound.

“You imagine I have sentenced myself?”

“Yes.”

“To what?”

“Survival without appeal.”

The room became utterly still.

Snape's eyes fixed on me.

I could not tell whether he hated me.

I could tell I had reached something true.

He stood.

His chair scraped stone.

“Enough.”

I nodded.

This time, I let him leave.

He returned two hours later carrying a paper-wrapped parcel.

He set it on my table.

“What is this?” I asked.

“Food.”

“I can see that.”

“Then your question is redundant.”

I unwrapped it.

Two meat pies. Still warm.

“You went to Hogsmeade?”

“Yes.”

“For pies?”

“No. I went to Hogsmeade to contemplate the unbearable persistence of your personality. The pies were incidental.”

I smiled.

He sat across from me.

Neither of us mentioned the argument.

We ate.

Halfway through, he said, “Hopkins was not the only one.”

I looked up.

Snape stared at his untouched second half of pie.

“There were students I could move. Students I could not. Punishments I could redirect. Others I could only shorten.”

His voice was controlled, but the words came slowly.

“I kept the Carrows from using certain curses in the Great Hall by convincing them public displays made the students less afraid, not more. I assigned Hagrid duties when I could. Filch when I could. I altered records so some detentions appeared completed.”

He swallowed.

“There were days when none of it mattered.”

I did not interrupt.

“There were children hurt in a castle I was supposedly running.”

“Were you supposed to be able to stop Voldemort alone?”

His lip curled. “Do not be ridiculous.”

“Then stop grading yourself on that standard.”

He looked at me sharply.

I took another bite of pie.

“Occupational hazard,” I said. “I recognize unreasonable quality control.”

His mouth twitched.

The room softened.

After lunch, we returned to work.

Near the end of the day, another former student passed the open door.

She was older than Hopkins, perhaps already graduated before the final year. She saw Snape and stopped.

Her expression held no gratitude.

Only anger.

“You,” she said.

Snape's face became blank.

“Yes.”

“You made my brother cry for two years.”

I went still.

She continued before anyone could stop her.

“You called him incompetent in front of everyone. He stopped taking Potions because of you. He wanted to be a Healer.”

Snape did not defend himself.

The woman waited.

So did I.

At last he said, “What was his name?”

She told him.

Recognition crossed his face.

“Yes,” he said.

The word was quiet.

“You remember?”

“Yes.”

“Well?”

Snape's hands tightened behind his back.

“I was cruel to him.”

The woman looked startled.

So was I.

He continued, each word precise.

“There was no educational justification for it. If he wishes to submit a formal complaint to the Board regarding my conduct, I will not contest the factual basis.”

Her anger shifted, not disappearing but losing its footing.

“He doesn't want a complaint.”

“Then I cannot offer him what he does not want.”

“You could apologize.”

Snape's face changed.

There it was again.

A silence that spoke.

He struggled.

Not because he did not know the word.

Because saying it would make the harm real in a different way.

“I am sorry,” he said.

The woman stared at him.

Then nodded once.

“I'll tell him.”

She walked away.

Snape did not move.

I looked down at my notes.

I gave him privacy without leaving.

Several minutes later, he said, “Do not.”

“Do not what?”

“Look pleased.”

I smiled at the parchment.

“I would never.”

“You are intolerable.”

“Accurate.”

He sat.

We finished the fluxweed in silence.

By then I knew enough to hear what he did not say.

After the woman left, Snape's hands remained motionless on the table.

I knew better than to ask who she was immediately.

Eventually he said, “Her son was in Slytherin.”

I waited.

“I accused him of attempting to attract attention when he reported harassment from older students.”

My stomach tightened.

“Were they harassing him?”

“Yes.”

The word was blunt.

“What happened?”

“I discovered it later. I punished them.” He looked at the fluxweed as if it were safer than my face. “By then he had learned something from me that I did not intend to teach.”

“What?”

“That asking for help was humiliating.”

There was nothing useful to say to that.

So I did not tell him he had been under pressure. I did not remind him of the war. I did not offer context he had not asked for.

“What would you do now?” I asked instead.

His eyes lifted.

“Believe the report long enough to investigate it.”

“Good.”

“Do not praise me for discovering the foundational principle of taking children seriously.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“You were thinking loudly.”

I smiled despite myself. “Maybe a little.”

He looked almost offended, which was better than looking hollow.

Sometimes it sounded very much like change.
